items.stem: The local council has ______ up a new scheme to encourage residents to recycle electronic waste.
items.explain: "Set up a scheme" is the correct collocation for creating or launching a programme. "Put up" means to accommodate or erect, and "make up" means to invent or reconcile.

items.stem: Despite the heavy rain, the outdoor concert went ahead and ______ out to be a huge success.
items.explain: "Turn out to be" means to unexpectedly result in being. "End up" is not followed by "to be", and "work out" without an object means to go well but does not take "to be".

items.stem: Not ______ did the documentary win several awards, but it also changed public opinion on marine conservation.
items.explain: Negative inversion at the start of the sentence ("Not only did... but it also...") requires "only" as the fixed correlative. The other options break the correlative structure.

items.stem: We had better leave for the station right away, ______ we might miss the last train home.
items.explain: "Otherwise" means "if not" and links the warning ("had better") to the possible consequence. "Unless" means "except if" and would reverse the meaning.

items.stem: The rapid ______ (GROW) of remote working has transformed the way modern offices are designed.
items.explain: Between the adjective "rapid" and the preposition "of" you need the abstract noun "growth". The classic trap is choosing "growing", which does not work as a noun here.

items.stem: "I am sorry I forgot to return your call yesterday," Clara said to Leo. (APOLOGISED) → Clara ______ Leo's call the previous day.
items.explain: The verb "apologise" takes the preposition "for" followed by a gerund ("for not returning"). Using an infinitive ("to not return" or "for not to return") is the classic grammar trap.

items.stem: It was a mistake not to back up the files before updating the system. (OUGHT) → We ______ up the files before updating the system.
items.explain: To express criticism or regret about the past, use "ought to have + past participle" ("ought to have backed"). "Ought to back" refers to the present, and omitting "to" is wrong.

items.stem: "When I first moved to the coastal village, I assumed the slow pace of life would drive me crazy within a month. Yet, instead of missing the city noise, I found myself dreading my occasional trips back to the capital." — What surprised the writer after moving?
options: How quickly the village became noisy in summer.
How easily she adapted to and preferred the quiet routine.
How difficult it was to travel back to the capital.
How unfriendly the local residents were at first.
items.explain: The text says she thought the slow pace would drive her crazy, but she ended up dreading trips back to the capital. The trap "city noise" appears literally but is negated by "instead of".

items.stem: "Although the new museum audio guide was praised by critics for its detailed historical commentary, most teenage visitors abandoned the tour halfway through, complaining it felt more like a university lecture than an interactive experience." — Why did teenagers dislike the audio guide?
options: The equipment stopped working halfway through.
The tone was too academic and lacked engagement.
The critics had given them false expectations.
items.explain: "Felt more like a university lecture than an interactive experience" means the tone was too academic and not engaging enough. "Halfway through" states when they gave up, not a fault.

items.stem: Many amateur runners believe that training harder every single day is the fastest route to a personal best. ______ Without those scheduled rest days, muscles cannot repair themselves and performance inevitably drops.
options: In fact, the opposite is often true when it comes to building endurance.
For this reason, professional athletes never take a break before a race.
This means that running shoes should be replaced every six months.
Similarly, swimming requires a great deal of upper-body strength.
items.explain: The next sentence uses "those scheduled rest days", which needs a prior contrast with "training harder every single day". "In fact, the opposite is often true" introduces that shift.

items.stem: A: "I joined for the flexible hours." | B: "I took the role purely for the high salary, though the shifts were brutal." | C: "The pay was modest, but the training was great." | D: "I wanted to work near home." — Which person initially accepted the job for financial reasons?
items.explain: Person B says "took the role purely for the high salary" (financial reason). Person C mentions "pay" as a lexical distractor but clarifies it was low ("modest").

items.stem: A: "The cast saved a weak script." | B: "Stunning visuals cannot rescue a predictable plot." | C: "Even though the storyline is familiar, the breathtaking photography alone makes the ticket worthwhile." | D: "The soundtrack was the only highlight." — Which reviewer recommends the film for its visual quality despite a predictable plot?
items.explain: Both B and C mention photography and a predictable plot, but only C recommends paying for the ticket ("makes the ticket worthwhile"). B says the opposite ("cannot rescue").
